newsitem.title: GERMANY: Europe-Iran ties in crisis after Berlin verdict.
newsitem.headline: Europe-Iran ties in crisis after Berlin verdict.

text.p: Relations between Tehran and Europe were in crisis on Friday after a German court accused Iran of ordering the killing of Kurdish dissidents in Berlin and indicated its highest leaders had sanctioned the attack.

Bonn ordered four Iranian diplomats out of the country and recalled its ambassador in Tehran for consultations after Thursday's verdict, which the German Foreign Ministry said portrayed a "flagrant violation of international law".
Germany also said it would no longer participate in a "critical dialogue" with Iran -- a European Union policy it has championed for years despite strong criticism from its allies.
Iran reacted to the verdict with similar measures -- withdrawing its ambassador and expelling four German diplomats.

The EU endorsed Germany's stance, inviting its members to also withdraw their top diplomats from Tehran for consultations and saying it did not see any room for critical dialogue while Iran "flouts international norms and indulges in acts of terrorism".
Swedish radio reported late on Thursday that Stockholm had ordered its ambassador to Teheran back home for consultations.
Washington encouraged the EU to pursue a policy of strong sanctions towards Iran and praised the court for its verdict.

Presiding judge Frithjof Kubsch said in his ruling that the assassination of four Kurdish Iranian leaders in 1992 was ordered by a secret special operations committee whose members included Iran's president, its religious leader, Intelligence Minister and the head of foreign policy.

He stopped short of explicitly naming Iranian President Ali Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani and religious leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who had been accused by prosecutors of ultimate responsibility for the attack in Berlin's Mykonos restaurant.

The verdict marked the first time a European court had clearly attributed political responsibility for any of the dozens of assassinations of Iranian opposition figures abroad since the Islamic revolution in 1979.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Mahmoud Mohammadi said the court verdict was unfounded and influenced by a propaganda campaign against Iran, the official IRNA news agency reported.
Mohammadi said the ruling had been made "in an unjust and biased manner based on the false claims of counter-revolutionary elements and hostile political propaganda of the Zionists".
Although Germany's reaction to the verdict contained strong language, it was delivered in the form of a faxed statement which also expressed the hope the situation would not escalate.

Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel declined all requests for interviews. He looked likely to find it more difficult to maintain a low profile on Thursday, with a host of photo opportunities on his daily schedule.

Germany has been a leading advocate of the EU's policy of critical dialogue with Tehran. The strategy has long been viewed with suspicion in Washington, which favours completely isolating Iran as an alleged perpetrator of international terrorism.

"The court's verdict corroborates our long-held view that Iran's sponsorship of terrorism is authorised at senior levels of the Iranian government," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters in Washington.
"The United States will maintain its own sanctions on Iran and we strongly encourage our European partners to do the same."
Outside the courtroom, sealed off to traffic and guarded by heavily armed police including roof-top snipers, more than 1,000 Iranian exiles cheered and danced when they heard the verdict.
"The Iranian political leadership ordered this crime," Kubsch said in his four-hour judgement. "This is an official liquidation measure ordered without a verdict."
"Decisions on such operations lie in the hands of the secret 'committee for special operations' which operates outside the constitution... There can be no lenience for state terrorism."
Bonn has warned German citizens not to travel to Iran in the next few days because of possible security risks.

Last November, after prosecutor Bruno Jost accused Iran's leaders of ordering the assassinations, an angry mob marched on the German embassy in Tehran, hurling eggs and stones and calling for Jost's death.

Kubsch handed down life sentences on Kazem Darabi, an Iranian, and Abbas Rhayel, a Lebanese, for the murders of Sadegh Sharafkandi, exiled leader of the Iranian Democratic Party of Kurdistan, and three other dissidents.
Two Lebanese received sentences of 11 years and five years and three months for complicity. A fifth suspect was cleared.
Of the Iranian leaders, Kubsch mentioned only one by name -- Intelligence Minister Ali Fallahiyan.
Fallahiyan had asked Bonn to put off the trial when he was received here just before it opened, and is now being sought on an arrest warrant for allegedly masterminding the murders.
